rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a story and a booby trap. It keeps the ClassPass temptation where it belongs — "The only supplied fact is that Mindbody owns ClassPass; how the assistant interacts with ClassPass inventory was not supplied" — while B turns that same gap into a headline: "Mindbody Owns the Studio Software, the Consumer Marketplace, and Now the AI That Fills Both." B has useful instincts, but A is the set a founder can take to a reporter without stepping on invented facts in sentence one.
gaps_in_A: "The software behind 50,000 studios wants AI to solve fitness's empty-slot problem" slightly rounds off the fact base: the update says over 50,000 studios and salons, and the category-level "empty-slot problem" needs outside context.
"a private owner doesn't have to show public markets an AI revenue line" is a smart thought, but still an inference; A flags that later, but the angle leans on a causal thread it cannot prove yet.
"What happened when a studio let an AI text its waitlist" is only usable if a named pilot studio exists; A says this, but it is still carrying a conditional angle as one of the kept angles.
gaps_in_B: "Mindbody Says AI Cut Fitness No-Shows by 22% — and It's Rolling Out to 50,000 Studios" invents rollout scale; the fact says Mindbody powers booking for over 50,000 studios and salons, not that this assistant is rolling out to all of them.
"While Fitness Apps Race to Build AI Coaches" imports an external trend not supplied in the update; that contrast needs proof before it becomes an angle, not after.

"Mindbody Owns the Studio Software, the Consumer Marketplace, and Now the AI That Fills Both" assumes ClassPass and the assistant fill the same inventory or slots. The update only gives ownership. That is the clever hallucination that gets a pitch killed.
"Bundled pricing / AI monetization angle — no_why_now_but_required" throws away a grounded monetization story while keeping the weaker speculative ClassPass platform story. Backwards triage.
